scenes.headline: How RF-DETR detects fast and sizes itself
scenes.sub: A DINOv2 backbone, set prediction, and one search that trains every size at once.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Quincy! RF-DETR is a real-time object detector. It predicts boxes in one shot, and it sizes itself from a single training run. Here's how.

scenes.text: One network is trained once. From it you pick any speed-accuracy point you want, with no retraining. The named sizes are just points on that curve.
scenes.say: The idea: train one network once, then pick any speed-accuracy point from it without retraining. The named sizes are just points someone chose on one curve.

steps.say: An image enters a DINOv2 backbone, a vision transformer pretrained on web-scale images.
It alternates cheap local windows with a few global layers, then a projector hands features to the decoder.
A fixed set of object queries read the features through deformable attention.

steps.note: each query claims at most one object
steps.say: Class and box heads give each query one label and one box. No suppression step. It's direct set prediction.

left.title: Old NAS
left.say: Normally you train a separate model for every size, and repeat the whole search for each new device.

right.title: Weight-sharing search
right.say: Here one shared network holds every config at once. Each step trains a random one. Afterward you grid-search the best, with no retraining.

steps.say: On COCO, every RF-DETR size sits above and to the left of the other detectors' curves.
Only the top curve crosses sixty. That corner is the largest size, the first real-time detector past sixty.

scenes.title: COCO accuracy, same harness
scenes.say: Re-measured in one harness, the largest size reaches sixty point one. The strong baselines stay below sixty, and even the nano hits forty-eight point four.

scenes.text: Train one shared network, then pick your operating point. That is how a detector family crossed sixty AP in real time.

recap: First real-time detector past sixty AP
scenes.say: To recap: a DINOv2 backbone, one-shot set prediction, one shared network for every size, and the first real-time detector past sixty.
